title: Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying, and Dividing Decimals

questions.prompt: When adding or subtracting decimals, always ___ the decimal points.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Never add or subtract decimals without aligning decimal points. [[imp:Decimal points must be in a vertical line.]]

formulaCard.title: Add/Subtract Decimals
notes: The decimal point is fixed; it's the columns that matter.
formulaCard.formula: Align decimal points, then operate. $$a.b + c.d = (a+c) + (b+d)$$ if aligned.

explanation: [[imp:1. Write the numbers vertically, aligning the decimal points. 2. Add or subtract as you would with whole numbers. 3. Bring the decimal point straight down into the answer. 4. Use placeholder zeros if needed.]]
For subtraction, the same rule applies: align decimal points, borrow if necessary.
Always round the answer to the desired place (e.g., nearest cent) if required.

visuals.caption: Decimal points aligned; zeros added for placeholders.
visuals.title: Adding Decimals

challengeCorner.prompt: A bill is \$78.56. You pay with \$100. How much change? Provide exact change in bills and coins.
hints: That's one \$20, one \$1, one quarter, one dime, one nickel, four pennies.

teacherCues: Write two decimal numbers vertically. Ask: 'Why must the decimal points align?'
Emphasize: Place value alignment is key.

discoveryHook.scenario: You buy cat food for \$12.45 and a toy for \$8.30. To find the total, line up decimal points and add: $12.45 + 8.30 = 20.75$. Adding decimals is just like adding whole numbers, but the decimal point stays in the same column.

blocks.title: 1. Adding & Subtracting Decimals

examples.title: B – Borrowing in subtraction
examples.peerPrompt: How do you handle the 0 in the hundredths place of 5.2?
steps: Borrow from the tenths: 2 becomes 1, hundredths becomes 10 → 10-7=3; tenths: 1-4 needs borrow from ones → 11-4=7; ones: 4-3=1.

examples.title: C – Real-world transaction
examples.prompt: You have \$50.00 and buy groceries for \$32.79. How much change?

blocks.title: 2. Multiplying Decimals

confusionCorner.body: When the product ends with zeros after the decimal, they may be dropped (e.g., 3.00 → 3). But for money, keep two decimal places. [[imp:Always check if rounding is required.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

hints: It separates whole from fractional part.
questions.prompt: To multiply decimals, count the total decimal places in the factors to decide where to put the ___ in the product.

hints: Multiplying by 100 moves decimal point two places right.

steps: Multiplying tenths by tenths gives hundredths.
The product of the digits is 24, but the value is tiny because both numbers are less than 1.
Counting decimal places ensures the product has the correct magnitude.
examples.title: B – Why count decimal places?

examples.prompt: Calculate the cost of 3.5 lbs of cat food at \$2.79 per lb.
examples.title: C – Multiply money

teacherCues: Show that multiplication ignores decimals until the final step.
Demonstrate how to count decimal places in factors to place the decimal point in the product.

discoveryHook.scenario: Amazon Prime costs \$14.99 per month. How much for a year? Multiply $14.99 \times 12 = 179.88$. The decimal point in the product is placed after counting the total decimal places in the factors.

explanation: [[imp:1. Multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers (ignore decimals). 2. Count the total number of decimal places in both factors. 3. Place the decimal point in the product so that it has that many decimal places.]]
Example: $14.99 \times 12$. 14.99 has 2 decimal places, 12 has 0 → product needs 2 decimal places → $179.88$.
If there are not enough digits in the product, add leading zeros to the left before placing the decimal point.
When multiplying by a whole number, the decimal point stays in the same position relative to the digits.

notes: Multiply ignoring decimals, then place the point based on total decimal places.
formulaCard.title: Decimal Multiplication
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Decimal places in product} = \text{sum of decimal places in factors}$$

visuals.title: Multiplying Decimals
visuals.caption: Count total decimal places in factors, apply to product.

confusionCorner.body: Only move the decimal point in the divisor and dividend equally. [[imp:Never move the decimal point in only one number; that changes the value.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

visuals.caption: Make the divisor a whole number, then divide.
visuals.title: Dividing Decimals

formulaCard.formula: $$a \div b = \frac{a \cdot 10^k}{b \cdot 10^k}$$ where $k$ shifts decimal of $b$ to make it whole.
notes: Move decimal points equally in dividend and divisor.
formulaCard.title: Decimal Division

explanation: [[imp:1. If the divisor is a whole number, divide as with whole numbers, placing the decimal point in the quotient directly above its position in the dividend.]]
[[imp:2. If the divisor has a decimal, move the decimal point to the right until it becomes a whole number; move the decimal point in the dividend the same number of places.]]
Add zeros to the dividend if needed to complete division.
Example: $3.6 \div 0.4$ → move decimal: $36 \div 4 = 9$.

blocks.title: 3. Dividing Decimals

discoveryHook.scenario: You spent \$179.88 for 12 months of Prime. How much per month? $179.88 \div 12 = 14.99$. Division revisits the original monthly cost. The decimal point in the quotient goes directly above the decimal in the dividend.

teacherCues: Teach division as making the divisor a whole number first.
Show how to move the decimal point in both dividend and divisor.

questions.prompt: When dividing by a decimal, move the decimal point in both numbers until the ___ becomes a whole number.

examples.title: A – Divide with whole number divisor

examples.peerPrompt: What happens when you shift the decimal point?
examples.title: B – Why move the decimal?
steps: Move decimal: $10 \div 2 = 5$. So there are 5 pieces of 0.2 in 1.
This is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal 5.
examples.prompt: Explain why dividing by 0.2 is the same as multiplying by 5.

discoveryHook.scenario: To convert meters to centimeters, multiply by 100 (move decimal two places right). To convert cents to dollars, divide by 100 (move decimal two places left). These shortcuts make decimal calculations instant.

questions.prompt: Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the ___.

examples.prompt: Explain how to convert 750 milliliters to liters by dividing by 1,000.
examples.title: B – Divide by 1000

blocks.title: 4. Shortcuts: Multiplying & Dividing by Powers of 10
teacherCues: Show how to move the decimal point instead of performing full multiplication/division.
Relate to place value: each power of 10 shifts digits one place.

challengeCorner.prompt: A worker earns \$15.50 per hour. How much does she earn for 10 hours of work? For 100 hours? Use shortcuts.

formulaCard.title: Powers of 10 Shift
notes: Add zeros as needed if there are not enough digits.
formulaCard.formula: $$a \times 10^n: \text{ move decimal } n \text{ places right}$$ $$a \div 10^n: \text{ move decimal } n \text{ places left}$$

visuals.caption: Moving the decimal point is faster than multiplying/dividing.
visuals.title: Powers of 10 Shortcuts

explanation: [[imp:Multiplying by 10, 100, 1,000... moves the decimal point to the right by 1, 2, 3... places.]]
[[imp:Dividing by 10, 100, 1,000... moves the decimal point to the left by 1, 2, 3... places.]]
Examples: $3.25 \times 10 = 32.5$ (one place right). $3.25 \times 100 = 325$ (two places right).
If you run out of digits, add zeros. $4.5 \div 100 = 0.045$ (shift left two places, add a zero).

confusionCorner.body: When moving the decimal point to the right, add zeros if there are no more digits. When moving left, add leading zeros. [[imp:Count the moves carefully; one extra or missing zero can change the value tenfold.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

questions.prompt: If €1 = \$1.10, to convert dollars to euros you ___ by the exchange rate.
Convert \$120 to euros if €1 = \$1.20. Round to nearest cent.
You have ¥5,000. 1 yen = \$0.0091. How many dollars? (Round to cent.)

teacherCues: Show a real currency exchange rate chart.
Explain that exchanging money involves multiplying or dividing by an exchange rate.

examples.title: A – Dollars to euros
steps: Rate is dollars per euro, so divide: $250 \div 1.08$.
The rate tells us 1 peso costs \$0.057.
To find how many pesos \$50 can buy, divide 50 by 0.057.
This gives the number of chunks of 0.057 in 50.
examples.prompt: Explain why converting \$50 to pesos (1 peso = \$0.057) involves division.
examples.title: B – Multiplication vs. division
examples.peerPrompt: Think: How many 0.057-dollar chunks are in 50 dollars?

examples.prompt: You return from Canada with 75 Canadian dollars. 1 CAD = \$0.74. How many U.S. dollars?
examples.title: C – Foreign to dollars

blocks.title: 5. Decimal Applications: Foreign Currency

challengeCorner.prompt: A trip to Europe: hotel costs €85 per night for 4 nights. €1 = \$1.09. Find the total hotel cost in dollars, rounded to the nearest cent.

confusionCorner.body: A common error is to multiply when you should divide. [[imp:Check: if the foreign unit is worth less than a dollar, you'll get more foreign currency than dollars, and vice versa.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

discoveryHook.scenario: You're traveling to Europe. The exchange rate is €1 = \$1.10. If you exchange \$500, you'll receive $500 \div 1.10 \approx 454.55$ euros. Decimals are essential for accurate currency conversion.

visuals.caption: Identify whether to multiply or divide based on the given rate.
visuals.title: Currency Conversion

explanation: To convert from one currency to another, you multiply or divide by the [[kw:exchange rate]].
If 1 unit of foreign currency = U.S. dollars, then: [[imp:Foreign amount × exchange rate = U.S. dollars]]. [[imp:U.S. dollars ÷ exchange rate = foreign amount]].
Example: €1 = \$1.10. \$500 to euros → $500 \div 1.10 = 454.545...$ ≈ €454.55 (rounded to nearest cent).
Always check whether to multiply or divide based on the direction of conversion.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Foreign} = \text{U.S.} \div \text{rate}$$ if rate is in U.S. dollars per 1 foreign unit. $$\text{U.S.} = \text{Foreign} \times \text{rate}$$
formulaCard.title: Currency Conversion Formulas
notes: Always round money to two decimal places.
